topic: Third-party requests: who is the client
stem: A professional women's soccer club has engaged a consultant to review how decisions about selection, rehab, and contracts get passed along inside the club. The written agreement calls for interviews across departments and a summary for the sporting director, with nothing attributed to a person. Her first interview is with Ifeoma, a striker who read the invitation and came willingly. Ifeoma sits down and says, "I've been dying for someone to work with. So this is my time?" Which reply describes the arrangement most accurately?
options: "The club is my client here, and what you tell me will feed my report, without your name."
"You're my client here, and the club will hear that we met and nothing more."
"Your coaches are my clients here, and what you tell me will help me advise them on working with you."
"You and the club are both my clients here, and you'll both approve what I write."
rationales: The club commissioned a review and receives the report, so the organization is the client and Ifeoma is an informant in it. Saying so before she shares anything is the third-party clarification the Ethics Code calls for.
This fits individual sessions arranged for a player. The agreement here calls for a report built from interviews, so telling Ifeoma nothing goes back would mislead her.
This fits a contract to advise the coaching staff. The agreement covers the whole club's communication and reports to the sporting director.
This fits a joint development plan with shared sign-off. Nothing in the agreement gives interviewees approval over the report.
takeaway: Who commissioned the work, for what purpose, and who gets the product tell you who the client is.

stem: For two years a consultant has seen university rowers one at a time. Now the head coach asks her to lead a weekly discussion series for the varsity crew at the boathouse, where rowers will talk about how they handle pressure and one another. She plans to reuse the written sheet from her individual work, which explains what coaches receive, how her notes are kept, and when safety overrides privacy. Which statement most needs to be added before the first meeting?
options: "Your parents may ask about our work, and I'll talk with you before I answer them."
"I'll keep what I hear private, and I can't promise that others who hear it will."
"Our connection is secure, and someone near you could still overhear or see your screen."
"A trainee will sit in with us, and I'll discuss our meetings with the trainee's mentor."
rationales: Parents' questions matter when clients are minors. These are university rowers, and nothing suggests parents have a part in the services.

The change from individual to group work adds a limit her sheet never needed: other participants hear every disclosure, and the consultant can't vouch for them. Group members need to know that before they share.
Overhearing and visible screens are limits of remote sessions. The crew is meeting face to face at the boathouse.
Clients should know about a trainee and supervision. No trainee is involved in this series.
takeaway: Moving from individual to group work adds a limit: the consultant can't guarantee other members' discretion.

stem: Wen, a 14-year-old figure skater, comes to a second meeting with her father, who signed the permission form last week. At the first meeting the consultant described sessions in plain terms, and Wen asked sharp questions about what her coach would hear. She took a week to think. Today she says, politely, "I get what it is. I don't want to do it." Her father says she'll warm up once things get going, and Wen shakes her head. What should the consultant do now?
options: Describe the work to Wen in plain terms, and ask whether she would like to take part
Ask her father for written permission, and go over with him what it covers
Start with an easy interview about skating, and ask at the end what she would like from the work
Put the work on hold for now, and let them both know that Wen can come back to it
rationales: Plain explanation and a request for assent come at the first meeting. Wen's questions and her week of thought show she already understands what is on offer.
Guardian permission is already in hand. What is missing is the young person's own agreement.
A light first interview is a sensible start once permission and assent are both present. Wen has understood the work and declined it.
Work with a minor rests on guardian permission plus the minor's assent. Wen gave an informed, considered no to an elective service, so the consultant respects it and leaves the way open.
takeaway: A minor's informed, considered refusal of elective work counts, even when a parent has signed.

stem: A consultant at a U.S. soccer academy wants a first picture of match nerves in an under-11 squad. Most of the boys came from Brazil with their families this fall. They joke freely in Portuguese during warm-ups and are in their school's beginner English class. Her shelf holds several questionnaires, all in English, and she can find no Portuguese version that has been tested with children. Which source of information should she rely on for now?
options: Interviews through a trained interpreter, with observation at matches
The SAS-2, completed by each player before an ordinary training session
The CSAI-2, completed by each player in the hour before a match
Short rating forms completed by the parents and the coach after matches
rationales: With no instrument supported for these children's language, the boys' own accounts through a trained interpreter, checked against observation, give the soundest information. Measures should suit both population and language.
The SAS-2 suits children who read English comfortably. Beginner English readers may not understand the items, so scores couldn't be trusted.
The CSAI-2 assesses state anxiety near competition, in English, and was developed with older competitors. It suits neither these boys' language nor their age.
Adult ratings help when children are too young to describe what they feel. These boys talk readily in Portuguese, so relying on outside impressions would skip the best source.
takeaway: When no instrument fits the client's age and language, interview and observe rather than score a poor fit.

topic: Assessment results and consent for use
stem: Before players on a junior hockey team (ages 18–20) filled out a mental skills inventory, each signed this: "My profile belongs to me. After my feedback meeting I'll decide what, if anything, goes to the player development coach." By November the consultant has finished the feedback meetings. Nineteen players wrote a page with her for the coach, and four preferred to keep theirs. The coach asks, "What can I have?" Which of these does the signed form let her hand over?
options: The team average for every scale, with no player identified
The scored profile for each player, marked for development use
A list of players who have finished the inventory and feedback
The pages written by the players who chose to pass one along
rationales: Group averages would be right if the form had promised staff team-level results. This form says nothing about averages and leaves each player to decide what goes out.
Full profiles would be right if players had agreed at testing that staff would receive them. Here the profile belongs to the player.
A completion list would be right if the form let staff know who took part. This one leaves what reaches the coach to each player, and no player chose to send that.
The form makes each player the one who decides, and nineteen decided to send a page. Sharing exactly that, and no one else's, matches what players consented to.
takeaway: Share assessment information in the form, and from the people, that the consent specifies.

topic: Intake: ordinary setback or clinical concern
stem: At intake with a consultant who isn't a licensed clinician, Desmond, a 52-year-old masters cyclist, says that dropping out of nationals last month "flattened" him. He skipped Sunday's club ride, slept badly for two nights, and told his wife he should take up lawn bowling. On Wednesday he joined the midweek group, got teased about it, "and gave it right back." He has slept fine since, has entered a race in May, and wants help with his nerves before long climbs. What is the best next step?
options: Recommend an evaluation with a licensed mental health professional
Continue the intake, and ask what he'd like from the work
Ask him directly whether he has had thoughts of suicide
Request a release to speak with the clinician who is treating him
rationales: An evaluation would be called for if low mood had lasted or spread through his life. A couple of bad days after a letdown, followed by a full return, is an ordinary reaction.
Desmond's reaction was brief, tied to one event, and has resolved; he is riding, sleeping, and planning. Nothing signals a need outside CMPC scope, so intake moves on to his goals.
A direct question is right whenever there is a sign of hopelessness or danger. His joke about bowling and quick return to friends and racing give no such sign.
A release is the way to coordinate with a treating clinician. Nothing in his account indicates that he has one or needs one.
takeaway: Brief, resolved distress after a setback is not a referral signal; watch duration, spread, and impairment.

stem: Halle, a 15-year-old swimmer at a club in the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement, has been quiet for two weeks. Today, sitting with the consultant on the bleachers in view of the pool deck, she pulls her towel tighter and says, "There's something about one of the grown-ups here. I want to tell you. But first swear it stays with you, or I'm not saying it." She looks at the consultant and waits. What should the consultant do at this moment?
options: Report to child protective services or police, and to the U.S. Center for SafeSport
Stay beside Halle, and call 911 so that an officer can come to the pool now
Check how Halle has been since the reports were made, and what support would help her
Tell Halle that some things can't stay secret, and that she is still welcome to talk
rationales: This is the prompt report required once there is reason to suspect abuse. Halle hasn't yet said what happened or who is involved; the question in front of the consultant is her request for a promise.
Emergency help is for immediate danger. Halle is in view of others and has described no present threat.
Follow-up support belongs after a report. No disclosure or report has been made.

An adult who may have to report can't promise secrecy. Saying so now, warmly and before Halle decides what to tell, is honest and keeps the conversation open; if she then discloses abuse, prompt reports follow.
takeaway: Never promise a minor secrecy; explain the limit before the disclosure, then report promptly if abuse is suspected.

stem: Thiago, a professional golfer on a developmental tour, wants to start weekly work in February. His money is tied up in entry fees, so he offers the consultant 5% of his winnings instead of her hourly rate. She explains that she can't tie her pay to his results. He nods and says, "Understood. My equipment company's check comes in July whether I win or not. I want to pay what your other clients pay. I just can't do it yet." Which arrangement fits best?
options: A lower fee, set by his current income and reviewed in the off-season
A set number of sessions without charge, agreed before he begins
Her usual fee, billed on fixed dates once he is able to pay
Her usual fee, billed to a sponsor under a written agreement
rationales: A sliding-scale fee is ethical and suits a client whose income is low for the foreseeable future. Thiago's shortfall ends in July, and he wants to pay the normal rate.
Pro bono sessions are ethical and suit someone who can't pay at all. Thiago can pay in full later in the year.
His difficulty is timing: guaranteed money arrives in July. Deferring a fixed fee answers that and keeps payment independent of results, as the Ethics Code requires.
Third-party payment is ethical when the payer agrees and roles are clear. The equipment company hasn't offered to pay for services; it simply pays Thiago.
takeaway: Fees can be reduced, waived, or deferred, as long as they don't depend on results.

stem: Harriet Blaise is ordering cards for a practice that opens on Monday. She finished a master's degree in counseling two years ago and earned the CMPC in the spring. Her state licensing application is in, and the board tells her that a decision usually takes three months. The last chapter of her doctoral dissertation is with her committee. Which line should she print?
options: Harriet Blaise, PhD, Certified Mental Performance Consultant
Harriet Blaise, MS, Licensed Professional Counselor, CMPC
Harriet Blaise, MS, Licensed Professional Counselor
Harriet Blaise, MS, Certified Mental Performance Consultant
rationales: The doctorate hasn't been awarded while the dissertation is still under review, so listing it would misstate her degree.
The certification and degree are accurate, but the license is still an application. Claiming it before it is granted would be a false public statement.
This line also claims a license she doesn't hold yet, and leaves off the certification she has earned.
A master's degree and the CMPC are what Harriet holds on the day the cards are printed. Public statements describe earned credentials, not pending ones.
takeaway: List only credentials you hold today; pending degrees and licenses wait.

stem: Cordelia, an airline executive, finished a year of work with a consultant three years ago and hasn't been in touch since. Reading that the consultant is opening a new practice, she emails a few unprompted lines for the website: the sessions "changed how I walk into a boardroom." She wants her name and job title on them, "because people in my world should know they can ask for this kind of help." What should the consultant do with the lines?
options: Publish them with her name, once she has approved in writing how they will appear
Thank her, and keep them off the website for the time being
Publish them without her name or title, once she has approved the wording
Ask her to take out the promise of results before they are published
rationales: The bar is on soliciting testimonials from current clients and others open to undue influence. Cordelia's work ended long ago, the offer was hers, and she wants to be named; written permission for the exact use completes it.
Holding the lines back would be right for someone still receiving services. Cordelia hasn't been a client for three years.
Leaving her name off suits a former client who wants to stay private. Being identified is the point Cordelia is making.
A guarantee of results would have to come out. Cordelia's lines describe her own experience and promise nothing to others.
takeaway: Testimonials: none from current clients; a former client's freely offered words need written permission and accuracy.

stem: A consultant at a small university sees most of the volleyball squad individually and enjoys the work. The head coach is adding a fourth vote to the staff meeting that picks each week's travel squad and tells him, "You know them better than any of us. Just give me your vote; you don't have to say why." The consultant is the only mental performance provider on campus and hopes to stay in that job. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Take it on, and explain the new duty to the athletes in writing
Take it on, and send the one athlete it affects to a colleague
Turn it down, and carry on with the consulting he does now
Turn it down, and hand the squad's consulting to someone else
rationales: Openness about a second role is enough when that role doesn't put anyone at risk. Judging his own clients for selection would compromise trust and objectivity however clearly it was announced.
Transferring a client can manage an overlap that touches one person. Most of the squad sees him, and no colleague is on campus to receive them.

Voting on clients' selection would draw on what they told him in confidence and make it risky for them to speak. A second role likely to impair the work or cause harm should be avoided, so he declines it.
Passing the squad to another consultant would help if his objectivity or the athletes' trust were already damaged. He hasn't voted, the work is going well, and nobody else on campus can do it.
takeaway: Some second roles can be managed openly; one that evaluates your own clients should be declined.

stem: In August the sports dietitian gave Tomás, a collegiate soccer player, an eating plan for adding muscle. He likes it, and at their November review she was pleased with his numbers and left it unchanged. On weekends he follows it easily. On days with back-to-back classes the afternoon snacks don't happen: "I pack them, I'm thinking about my lab, and at six they're still in my bag." He asks the consultant what to do. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Connect him with the sports dietitian about changing the plan
Work with him on goals and cues for following the plan
Connect him with the team physician for an evaluation
Connect him with a campus counselor for an evaluation
rationales: The dietitian would set or change what he eats. She reviewed the plan and Tomás likes it; what breaks down is remembering it on crowded days.

Forgetting an agreed behavior on busy days is a self-regulation problem, and goal setting, cues, and implementation plans are squarely within CMPC scope. The content of the plan stays with the dietitian.
A physician would be needed for physical symptoms or unexpected changes. His numbers pleased the dietitian, and he reports no symptoms.
A counselor would be needed for warning signs of a disorder. A snack forgotten while thinking about a lab, with no distress about food, isn't one.
takeaway: What to eat belongs to the dietitian; helping a client follow through on it is mental skills work.

stem: In March, Rosamund, a CMPC, told another CMPC over coffee that his podcast had given away a client's identity. He thanked her and cut the segment. In summer he told two more recognizable client stories, and she went back to him with the passages marked. He said listeners love them and he would go on telling them. He works alone. Yesterday's public episode gives a client's team, jersey number, and medical history. What is Rosamund's most appropriate next step?
options: File a written complaint with the AASP Ethics Committee
Raise the episode with him privately, and ask him to take it down
Describe the situation to a mentor without names, and ask whether it breaches the Code
Bring it to the person who supervises him
rationales: Informal resolution comes first, and she has tried it twice. He refuses and the disclosures are growing more serious, so a formal route to the Ethics Committee is now appropriate.
A private talk is the usual starting point. Two of them have already taken place, and after the second he told her he would continue.
A mentor's view helps when it is unclear whether a standard was broken. Identifying clients with medical details on a public show is clearly a breach.
A supervisor is the right contact when the colleague is a trainee or employee. He is an independent practitioner with nobody over him.
takeaway: Try informal resolution first; when it fails and harm continues, go to the Ethics Committee.

stem: A consultant (CMPC, not a licensed provider) drafts a plan for Ana, 13, at a gymnastics club in the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement. Text reminders will go to a thread with Ana and her mother. On Thursdays they'll talk in a staff room off the back hallway during practice, blinds drawn so that teammates don't stare. Ana will ride to regionals in the team van with two coaches and the squad. They'll debrief over the team breakfast at the hotel. Ana's mother approves it all in writing. Which part needs to change?
options: The text reminders during the week
The ride to regionals in the van
The Thursday talks during practice
The debrief at the team hotel
rationales: Messages to a minor are fine when they are professional and a parent is on the thread, as Ana's mother is.
A van carrying two coaches and the whole squad isn't a one-on-one situation, so this travel is appropriate.

A room off the back hallway with the blinds drawn can't be observed, and a parent's signature doesn't waive the MAAPP expectation that one-on-one meetings be observable and interruptible. A spot in view but out of earshot would protect both privacy and safety.
Breakfast with the team present is in plain view and easy to interrupt, so the hotel setting isn't a concern here.
takeaway: One-on-one time with a minor athlete stays observable and interruptible, whatever a parent has signed.

stem: Lorna, 61, took up trail running for her health and would like three sessions on race-day nerves. She is short of cash until spring. A potter, she suggests that the consultant pick a piece off her shelf at the county gallery, where one she likes is tagged at the price of three sessions. People in their valley commonly settle bills this way. The two women know each other only by sight, and Lorna says it makes no difference to her if the consultant prefers cash in spring. What is the best response?
options: Take the piece as a thank-you gift, and make a note of it in the file
Turn it down, and offer her a reduced fee until spring
Take the piece as payment, with the terms in writing
Turn it down, and refer her to a colleague in town
rationales: A small token at the end of paid work can be accepted as a gift. This is payment for services, and recording it as a gift would disguise the fee.
Offering another fee arrangement is right when a trade would be unfair or would entangle the work. Here the value is public, the exchange is single, and Lorna is free to pay otherwise.

Barter is acceptable when it isn't contraindicated or exploitative. A posted price equal to the fee, one completed exchange, local custom, and no pressure on Lorna meet those conditions, and written terms make the agreement clear.
Referral fits when an existing relationship would compromise the work. They know each other only by sight.
takeaway: Barter isn't banned: it must be fair, non-exploitative, harmless to the work, and clear.

stem: A mother calls a consultant who holds the CMPC and no license. Her 16-year-old son, Emrys, is a pole vaulter. In practice he clears his heights; at big meets his hands go cold, he hurries his run, and he passes early. "The rest of the time he's just Emrys," she says: grades steady, friends in and out of the house, asleep by ten. He laughs about it himself. His sports physical was clean. She asks, "Is this a psychologist's job? A doctor's? Yours?" Which answer is most accurate?
options: "I can help him with that directly; it's the kind of work I do with athletes."
"A licensed psychologist should see him first and assess what's behind it."
"His doctor should see him first and look for a physical cause."
"He should stay with his therapist, and I can add performance work alongside."
rationales: Nerves confined to big meets in a teenager who is otherwise doing well are a performance concern, which mental performance consulting addresses. The consultant can say so plainly and describe what the work does and doesn't include.
Assessment by a psychologist would come first if distress had spread into school, sleep, or friendships. All of those are going well.
A doctor would come first if symptoms were new, unexplained, or happening outside meets. The physical was clean, and cold hands come only with big meets.
Work alongside treatment suits a client who is already in therapy. Emrys has no therapist, and nothing his mother describes suggests that he needs one.
takeaway: Competition-bound nerves in a well-functioning client are within CMPC scope; say so without over-referring.

stem: A consultant ran a program for club swimmers aged 10 to 13 last spring. Her folder from it holds the attendance sheets and a survey that parents completed after the final session, in which 41 of 48 families said they'd enroll again. The studies she draws on were carried out with university and national-team swimmers. Her brochure for this year's parents has room for one line about how the program has done or what supports it. Which line could she print as it stands?
options: "Most of last spring's families told us they would enroll again."
"Last spring's swimmers were racing faster by the end of the program."
"Studies with swimmers your child's age support the skills we teach."
"Last spring's swimmers were using more mental skills by the end."
rationales: The survey supports exactly this and no more, so the claim is accurate. Public statements should go no further than the data behind them.
Race times would support this line. Her folder holds attendance and a parent survey, neither of which measures speed.
Research with children would support this line. The studies she uses tested university and national-team swimmers.
A measure of skill use before and after would support this line. Nothing in the folder measured what swimmers did.
takeaway: Advertise what your data show, even when the true claim is the modest one.

stem: Florian, an adult triathlete, worked weekly with a consultant for one season. They held a final review and said goodbye three years ago. Since then he has booked two single sessions to rework his swim start, the more recent of them fourteen months ago, and he has none planned. He writes now to say that he thinks about her and would like to take her to dinner, as a date. She is single and likes him. Which limit settles her reply?
options: The bar on intimacy with someone who is a client at present
The waiting period that runs from the end of services
The duty to show that intimacy would not be exploitative
The bar on consulting with a past intimate partner
rationales: This would govern if services were continuing. Florian has had no session for fourteen months and has none planned, so he is a former client.
Services last took place fourteen months ago, not three years ago, because the single sessions were services. Intimacy with a former client is barred for at least two years, so she declines.
Showing that a relationship wouldn't exploit him becomes the question only after at least two years have passed since services ended.
This would govern if the two had once been partners and he now wanted to be a client. The order here is the reverse.
takeaway: The two-year minimum runs from the last service, including a one-off session.

stem: Tamsin, a high school basketball player, strained her hamstring five weeks ago. Her athletic trainer cleared her on Tuesday and, when Tamsin asked for another check this morning, found full strength and no pain. She can't wait for Friday's game. "I know it's fine. I ran full length for an hour," she tells the consultant. "Then I go to cut hard and my brain hits the brakes." What is the most appropriate response?
options: Ask her to have the athletic trainer check her leg again
Rehearse hard cuts with her in imagery before the game
Help her weigh whether she wants to play on Friday
Suggest that she talk with her coach about shorter minutes
rationales: Another check would be needed if she reported a new sensation. The trainer found nothing this morning, and what stops her happens in her head.
The medical decision has been made by those who own it. What remains is fear of reinjury on one movement, and rehearsing it with confidence is mental skills work within scope.
Weighing the decision would help a player who was torn about returning. Tamsin can't wait to play.
Shorter minutes would make sense if her conditioning were lagging. She ran full length for an hour.
takeaway: Once medical staff clear an athlete, the remaining fear of reinjury is within the consultant's scope.

stem: A professional symphony asks a consultant to coach its string players for a round of chair auditions that begins in eleven days. Her entire career has been in team sports. She has never attended an audition, doesn't know how playing-related injuries show up, and has no mentor in the performing arts. Two members of her peer group have worked with orchestras for years, and one of them mentioned being free this month. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Accept, and prepare with reading and a performing-arts mentor
Accept, and adapt her existing program
Pass the request to the colleague who works with orchestras
Accept the general workshop, and leave the coaching to others
rationales: Building competence through study and mentoring is how to enter a new field when there is time. Eleven days before players' jobs are at stake leaves none.
Adapting an established program suits a consultant with experience of this work. Her career has been in team sports.
She lacks the competence, can't gain it in eleven days, and knows a qualified person who is free. Competence and concern for the musicians' welfare both point to handing this one over.
Taking only the part she can do well works when the request has such a part. The symphony asked for audition coaching.
takeaway: When there's no time to build competence and a qualified colleague is available, pass the work on.

stem: Ilya plays tennis in a U.S. Olympic and Paralympic movement program. Since he was 16 he has exchanged pre-match messages with the consultant on a thread that includes his father. The two of them have always kept it short and professional. Last month Ilya had a birthday, signed his own consent form, and registered to vote. He now asks, "Can we take my dad off? Some of what I'd like to say before matches is just for us." How should the consultant handle the messages?
options: Move to direct messages, with limits on timing and content
Keep his father on the thread, and explain why
Move his reminders to the squad thread, with the coaches included
Stop messaging between sessions, and go over reminders in person
rationales: Copying a parent protects minors. Ilya can now vote and has signed for himself, so he is an adult client, and messaging can be private between them under agreed professional limits.
Keeping a parent copied, with an explanation, is right for a minor. Ilya's birthday and signature show that he isn't one any longer.
A squad thread suits reminders meant for everyone. He wants to say things that are for the consultant alone.
Ending messages would fit if the program barred them or if they had become a problem. They have been brief and professional.
takeaway: MAAPP's transparency rule for messages protects minors; adult clients get private, professional channels.

stem: In September a consultant who isn't a clinician noticed that Simone, a collegiate diver, was losing weight and skipping meals. She told Simone, and Simone went to sports medicine. Since then a physician, dietitian, and therapist have treated her, with releases signed for all three. This week the physician cleared her for full training, and the therapist wrote that she is doing well. Simone comes in smiling, mentions the breakfast she cooked, and says she keeps balking on her inward dives. What should the consultant do in this session?
options: Tell Simone privately what she has noticed about her eating
Help Simone set up a visit with sports medicine
Work with Simone on the balk in her inward dives
Ask Simone for a release to speak with her therapist
rationales: Voicing concern in private was the right step in September. Today there is nothing new to notice: she is eating, cleared, and doing well.
Connecting her with sports medicine was the right step once the concern was raised. She is already under its care.

The disorder is being treated by those qualified to treat it, and they have cleared her. Balking on a dive is a performance concern she has brought herself, so the consultant works on it and leaves eating to the treatment team.
A release was needed before coordinating care. It has been signed, and the therapist is already writing to the consultant.
takeaway: When clinicians are treating the disorder and the client is cleared, do the performance work you were asked for.

stem: A technology company's leadership office has sent a consultant a list of four requests. She was a licensed psychologist in a hospital mood clinic for nine years, where she also ran stress groups, and her license is current. She then retrained, earned the CMPC, and has spent three years preparing surgeons and athletes for high-pressure days. Which of the requests lies furthest outside the competence her background supports?
options: Evaluating a manager who has asked whether he is depressed
Preparing a vice president for a series of hostile investor calls
Recommending how to combine three overlapping departments
Leading a small group on recovering between long workdays
rationales: Evaluation for depression is beyond most mental performance consultants. This one holds a current psychology license and nine years of experience with mood disorders.
Preparing someone for high-pressure events is what she has done for surgeons and athletes since earning the CMPC.

Nothing in her clinical or performance training prepared her to redesign an organization. Competence is judged against the individual's own education and experience, so this is the piece to pass to a specialist.
She has led stress groups and knows recovery, so a small-group session on it fits both parts of her background.
takeaway: Competence is individual: check the request against this consultant's training, not against a job title.

stem: Three weeks before a qualifying event, an elite wheelchair tennis player brings her consultant a study: 18 college basketball players improved at free throws with a new visualization method, and there was no comparison group. The consultant has read the paper closely and found nothing that follows it up. The player has held her serve well all spring with the routine they built together. "Should we switch?" she asks. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Switch to the new method, and drop the routine they built
Add the new method to the routine, and track her serve
Keep the routine, and explain what the study can't show
Read the study's methods, and bring her an answer next week
rationales: A switch would be reasonable if her routine were failing and the method were well supported for players like her. Neither is so.
A tracked addition is a reasonable off-season experiment. Three weeks before a qualifier, with serves holding, it puts a working routine at risk on thin evidence.

An uncontrolled study of 18 college players in another task can't show that the method works, still less that it beats what is working for her now. Evidence-informed practice weighs research against this client's results and timing.
Reading the paper first would be responsible if she hadn't. She has read it and looked for follow-ups.
takeaway: Weigh a new finding against its design, its fit, and how well the current plan is working.

stem: A consultant is employed by a university athletic department. The consent form tells athletes that the department may review records "to the extent needed to confirm that services were provided." An internal auditor writes that she is checking whether the 212 hours charged to the mental performance budget last year actually took place, and asks for "whatever you have." Which records should the consultant send?
options: Session dates and lengths, listed by client code
A summary of common themes, with nobody named
Notes from the sessions listed in a signed release
The complete file, sent by a secure transfer
rationales: The consent form ties review to confirming that services happened. Dates and lengths answer that, and codes keep identities out, so this is the least disclosure that serves the purpose.
Unnamed themes would inform planning. They reveal what athletes talk about and don't show whether 212 hours took place.
Released notes are what an athlete's chosen recipient would receive. No athlete has signed one here, and content isn't needed to count hours.
A whole file might go to a new provider at the athlete's request. The auditor's question doesn't require it, and the form doesn't allow it.
takeaway: Disclose the least that the stated purpose and the consent allow.

topic: Release of information to another provider
stem: In March, Liam, a 27-year-old professional rugby player, signed a release good through September. It names his grief counselor and covers "what we're aiming for in rugby and how often we meet." In July the counselor calls the consultant. Liam seems worn out, she says, but he isn't in any danger; she hears little from him about match nights and wonders what he has been saying on that subject. What may the consultant share on this call?
options: What Liam has said in their sessions about match nights
Nothing about the work until Liam signs a fresh release
Details about the risk to Liam, as far as safety requires
The purpose of the performance work and its schedule
rationales: Session content would be open if the release had covered it. Liam's covers aims and frequency, and the counselor's interest doesn't widen it.
Silence would be right after September or if Liam had withdrawn the release. In July it is still in force.
Disclosure to protect safety is a separate exception. The counselor reports no danger, and nothing suggests one.
The release is current, names this counselor, and covers these two things. The consultant shares what it authorizes and can tell Liam about the counselor's question.
takeaway: Read a release for who, what, and until when, and share exactly that.

stem: A consultant whose softball career ended when knee surgery failed sees that her first client today, Xiomara, has the same injury. She feels her throat tighten over the intake form. In the session Xiomara, a collegiate shortstop recovering well, goes silent and then says, for the first time to anybody, "I don't think I'll trust it again." Her eyes fill, and she looks away. Which response is most appropriate?
options: "I had that surgery too, and I remember that feeling."
"You're not sure you can rely on it the way you did."
"On which rehab days has it felt most like yours?"
"What has your surgeon said about how it's holding up?"
rationales: A brief disclosure can help when it serves the client and the story is settled for the teller. The consultant's is still raw and ended badly, so it risks shifting the focus to her.
Xiomara has just voiced something new and painful. Reflecting it lets her stay with it, and keeps the consultant's unresolved experience from entering the session to meet her own need.
Looking for better days can build hope once a client feels heard. Asked at the moment she first says this aloud, it moves past the feeling.
The surgeon's view would matter if she were asking about the graft. She is telling the consultant how she feels.
takeaway: Before disclosing, ask whose need it meets; if the experience is still raw, stay with the client's.

stem: A professional baseball organization invites its consultant to sit in on contract meetings and comment on players' "mental toughness." She sees a problem, marks the Ethics Code standards and contract clauses that bear on it, and talks it over with her mentor without naming players. Between them they come up with three responses: turn the invitation down, attend for staff matters only, or propose a separate education session. Following a structured ethical decision-making model, what should she do next?
options: Work out how each response would affect those concerned
Talk the situation through with a trusted mentor
Establish which standards and agreements apply
Write up how it turned out and what she learned
rationales: She has identified the issue, checked the standards, consulted, and generated responses. Weighing the likely consequences of each for players, staff, and the organization comes before choosing and acting.
Consultation is an early safeguard in these models. She has had that conversation.
Identifying standards comes near the start. She marked the Code and contract passages before talking to her mentor.
Documenting the outcome closes the process. No response has been chosen or carried out.
takeaway: Identify, check standards, consult, generate options, weigh consequences, act, evaluate.

stem: A consultant is starting a first video session with Arjun, a firefighter in another state. His signed forms give his home address, a neighbor as his emergency contact, and his cell number, which she has just called to help him log in. She matched his ID on the screen. He isn't at home: he is in the cab of his parked truck, alone, on the way back from a wildfire deployment, and he is eager to begin. What does the consultant most need to ask before the intake?
options: "What is your exact location right now?"
"Is there anybody close enough to hear us?"
"Could you hold your ID up to the camera?"
"What number should I use if we get cut off?"
rationales: Emergency help has to be sent to where the client is. The address on file is no longer where Arjun is sitting, so the consultant needs his actual location before starting.
Privacy would be the concern if others were around. Arjun is alone in a closed cab.
Identity should be verified at a first session. She has already matched his ID.
A backup number is part of the disconnection plan. She has his cell number and has just reached him on it.
takeaway: Confirm the client's physical location at every remote session; the address on file may not be it.

stem: A consultant wants intake information from 30 university athletes who are spread across the country for the summer and report to campus in two weeks. Her questionnaire covers injury history, sleep, and mood. She'll use it to decide whom to call in the first days and to plan each athlete's opening session. The department gives her an encrypted platform that only she can open. Which way of collecting the information fits best?
options: An anonymous questionnaire filled out on the platform
A paper questionnaire completed in a private room
A video interview based on the questionnaire
A named questionnaire filled out on the platform
rationales: Anonymous answers encourage candor when only group patterns matter. She needs to know whose mood or sleep calls for a prompt contact.
Paper in a private room works when athletes are on campus. They are scattered across the country.
Interviewing each athlete would give depth in a small group. With 30 athletes and two weeks, it would delay learning whom to call first.

She has to connect answers to people in order to follow up and plan, and has to reach them remotely. Named responses in an encrypted system that only she can open meet both needs with protection suited to sensitive data.
takeaway: Let the purpose decide whether data need names, then protect them accordingly.

stem: Before he has met the players, a consultant for a professional basketball team gets a file from the performance staff with each player's sleep and heart-rate variability. The consent form players signed in preseason reads: "My nightly data go to the performance staff and the mental performance consultant for planning my support. I can opt out of either by checking a box." Two players checked the consultant's box; their rows are in the file as well. First meetings begin on Monday. What should he do?
options: Set the file aside until players have been asked about his access
Use the file to prepare, after removing the players who opted out
Use the team averages to prepare, and leave individual rows unopened
Send the file back, and collect his own sleep ratings on Monday
rationales: Waiting would be right if players hadn't known about his access. The form named the consultant and the purpose, and players had the chance to refuse.
Players were told who would see the data and why, and most agreed. Honoring the form means using what they agreed to share and taking out the two who declined.
Averages alone would be right if the form had limited him to group data. It speaks of planning each player's support.
Collecting his own ratings would help if the device data were doubtful. Nothing suggests that they are.
takeaway: Consent defines the use of wearable data: honor both the yes and the opt-out.

stem: A consultant leads weekly video sessions on handling pressure for a sales team that works from home. Members join by personal links from a waiting room, and at the first session they settled how to treat one another's stories. After the third session Iolanthe, a member, forwards an email from the company's meeting service: "Here's your recap!" It contains much of what she said, word for word. The sales director, who scheduled the series, is copied. What should the consultant do first?
options: Have members revisit what they settled about repeating stories
Shut off the automatic notes, and have the saved copies removed
Have members confirm at the start of each session that they are alone
Give each member a new link, and admit members one by one
rationales: Revisiting group norms fits when a member has passed something along. No member did; the software sent the email.
The meeting service is recording what members say and delivering it to someone outside the group. Stopping it and removing what it has saved closes the actual leak.
Checking for others in the room fits when somebody has overheard. A verbatim text sent to the director didn't come from a listener at home.
New links fit when an uninvited person has got in. Members already use personal links and a waiting room.
takeaway: In online groups, check what the platform itself records and who receives it.

stem: When they began, the consultant and Camille, an elite fencer, put in writing that messages on the secure app are for training notes, that he answers by ten the next morning, and that anything urgent means a call. Camille has used it well for months. At 11:40 tonight she sends a long, cheerful account of a new parry, with questions, and at midnight adds, "Hello?? Are you there? I'm wide awake thinking about this!" The consultant happens to see both. What is the best response?
options: Answer in the morning, as he would another training note
Talk with her about what messages are for and how soon he replies
Call her now, and ask how she is and whether she's safe
Suggest that she keep these notes in a journal
rationales: The message is a training note sent late at night, and the agreement already says when it will be answered. Keeping to it maintains a boundary that has been working.
That conversation sets expectations when none exist or when they've stopped working. They are in writing, and one impatient message after months isn't a breakdown.
A call is right when a message hints at danger. Camille is excited about a parry.
A journal suits reflections that don't need a reply. She is asking questions, which is what the app is for.
takeaway: A messaging agreement works when you keep to it; an eager note isn't an emergency.

stem: Midway through a video session Corinne, a police officer, speaks of a call that went badly last week. "I don't see the point of any of it anymore," she says, and her picture freezes and drops. She has never spoken this way before, and the consultant hasn't yet been able to ask what she means. Thirty seconds pass. The plan they wrote at intake lists her cell number, her sister's number, and the emergency services where she takes her sessions. What should the consultant do first?
options: Contact emergency services where Corinne takes her sessions
Call Corinne's sister, and ask her to go over
Call Corinne on the number she gave for dropped sessions
Send Corinne a new link, and stay in the session until she joins
rationales: Emergency services are the step for stated intent, or for a worrying call when she can't be reached. Nobody has yet tried to reach her, and her meaning isn't known.
Her sister is a next contact if Corinne doesn't answer. Going to her first would disclose the situation before the direct route has been tried.
Corinne's words need a prompt safety conversation, and the quickest way to have one is the backup number. If she doesn't answer, the plan moves on to others and to emergency services.
Resending a link and waiting suits an ordinary session. After what she said, the consultant should actively reach her.
takeaway: After a worrying drop, call the backup number at once, and escalate if you can't reach the client.

stem: Before the season, a consultant plans how to evaluate her work with a university lacrosse team online. Last year she used the same ratings in August and May, saw the team average stay flat, and couldn't tell whether nobody had changed or whether some had climbed while others had slid. Several players also told her, kindly, that they'd rated her higher than they felt because their names were on it. Which design for this year best addresses both problems?
options: Surveys in both months with no identifying information
Surveys in both months linked by a code only the player knows
Surveys in both months with names, seen only by the consultant
Group discussions in both months led by a colleague from elsewhere
rationales: Dropping all identifiers would bring candor. It would leave her again with averages and no way to follow a player from August to May.
A self-made code lets each player's two sets of ratings be matched without revealing who the player is, so she sees individual change and players can be frank.
Names would show who changed. They are also what led players to soften their ratings last year.
An outside discussion leader can draw out frank, detailed views. It wouldn't show how far each player's ratings moved.
takeaway: Self-generated codes give matched data and anonymity when you need both.

stem: Gustavo, a masters rower, has used slow-paced breathing for six weeks to manage race nerves. The app shows that he practiced on 40 of 42 days. His watch's overnight heart-rate variability hasn't moved. At both regattas in that time, a chest strap worn on the dock showed a heart rate well below last year's at the same events, and his nerves rating fell from 8 to 4. His training and fitness are about what they were. Which reading fits these data best?
options: The breathing has calmed how he feels and left his body's response as it was
The breathing hasn't been practiced enough for its effects to be judged
The breathing has improved his recovery, which has made races feel easier
The breathing has eased his response before races, with recovery unchanged
rationales: This would fit a lower rating with no physical change on the dock. The strap showed a markedly lower heart rate there.
This would fit a sparse practice log. He practiced on nearly every day.
This would fit a rise in overnight variability alongside calmer races. Overnight variability stayed flat.

Ratings and dock heart rate both changed at the moment he was targeting, and the overnight measure, which reflects recovery, didn't. Each measure speaks to its own situation, so a flat overnight line doesn't cancel the race-day change.
takeaway: Match the measure to the target: overnight HRV says little about arousal on the start line.

stem: A new consultant recorded a video session with Osgood, a collegiate wrestler, under a consent form that says the recording is for review with her mentor and will be erased within 30 days. She and the mentor went through it on day nine. It is now day 29. She thinks it is the best session she has done and would love to study it again. Osgood graduated last week and hasn't replied to the note she sent him about it. What should she do with the recording?
options: Ask Osgood to agree to a longer period, and keep it until he replies
Move it to encrypted storage, and keep it with his other records
Erase it by the end of tomorrow, and note the date in his client record
Send it to her mentor by secure link, and ask for a second review
rationales: Asking for a longer period is reasonable while the agreed time is still running. She has asked, had no reply, and can't extend the consent by waiting.
Secure storage with the file would be right if the form had promised that the recording would be kept. It promised the opposite.
The form set purpose and time limits. The review is done, the time is nearly up, and no new consent has come, so she keeps the promise he agreed to.
A secure transfer for mentor review would fit if the review hadn't taken place. It took place on day nine.
takeaway: Recording consent includes an end date; honor it even when the recording is useful.

stem: Seung-ho, a 22-year-old professional esports player, is a current client. On his public stream he tells viewers that he has been working on his nerves "with a really good mental performance coach" and tags the consultant's professional page. He mentions nobody else, and he never told her he was going to do it. Fans start asking under the clip whether it's true. What should the consultant do?
options: Reply under the clip with a short thank-you
Repost the clip on her page with his written permission
Ask him to take the clip down before more people see it
Leave the clip alone, and talk with him about it next session
rationales: A public thank-you would be fine for something that involves no client, such as praise for a talk she gave. Here it would confirm a confidential relationship.
A former client's freely offered praise may be shared with permission. From a current client, promoting it would turn his remark into a testimonial.
Removal would be worth asking for if the clip exposed someone else's confidences. His own story is his to tell.
Clients may disclose their own consulting; the consultant's duty of confidentiality still holds. She neither confirms nor uses the clip, and they discuss what it means for him and the work.
takeaway: A client may go public about your work; you still don't confirm it or use it.

stem: A consultant with an office in Colorado hears from Maja, a professional golfer from Sweden who wants weekly video sessions for twelve weeks, starting in January. Maja plays a European schedule most of the year, keeps her apartment in Gothenburg, and will pay from her Swedish bank. Each winter, from New Year until April, she rents a house in Arizona and trains there. The consultant will work from her office throughout. Whose rules on practice and titles should the consultant look into first?
options: Those of Colorado and Sweden
Those of Arizona and Sweden
Those of Colorado alone
Those of Colorado and Arizona
rationales: This pairing would apply if Maja were at home in Gothenburg during the sessions. Residence and bank account don't place her there from January to April.
This pairing would apply if the consultant were working from Arizona and Maja from Sweden. The consultant stays in her Colorado office.
A single state's rules would apply if both were in Colorado during the sessions. Maja will be in Arizona.
Remote services are governed by the law where each party is located when they take place. For these twelve weeks that means a consultant in Colorado and a client in Arizona.
takeaway: For remote work, check the law where both parties are physically located during sessions.

stem: A clip of a quarterback's outburst on the sideline goes viral. A radio host who has had a consultant on air twice before to talk about pressure invites her back: the segment will play the clip and ask her, step by step, what was going on with him. The quarterback has been seeing her privately since spring and has told no one. The host knows nothing about this and needs an answer within the hour. What is the most appropriate reply?
options: Accept, and speak about pressure in general without mentioning him
Decline, and pass along the statement that he has approved
Accept, and ask the host to correct how she was introduced last time
Decline, and leave the reason for it unspoken
rationales: General education is a good use of a media invitation when the topic is general. This segment is built around his clip, so anything she says will be heard as about him, from what she knows in confidence.
A client can authorize a specific statement. He has told nobody about the work, there's no sign that he has approved anything, and passing it along would reveal the connection.
Correcting a misstatement of one's credentials is a duty when one has been made. Nothing like that has come up here.
He is a client, so commenting would draw on confidential knowledge, and explaining why she can't would reveal it. A plain no protects both the relationship and the fact of it.
takeaway: When the subject is secretly your client, decline without a reason; the reason itself is confidential.

stem: A consultant's newsletter goes to coaches throughout a small national track program. For the next issue she wants an example of a routine that settled panic about lane draws. She has seen it once in her career, with Abebe, a 24-year-old steeplechaser who is a current client and keeps that private. When she asked him about it he said, "I'd rather not be in there. Even as a mystery guy, they'd know in a second." Which example should she use?
options: A composite drawn from several clients, with details altered
An invented athlete, labeled for readers as made up
Abebe's story, with the wording he has signed off on
Abebe's story, with his name and event left out
rationales: Composites protect people when many clients share an experience. Only Abebe has had this one, so a composite would still be him.
Abebe declined and would be recognized in any version of his story. A clearly labeled fictional example teaches the same lesson and discloses nothing about him.
His story would be usable with specific written consent. He was asked and said no.
Removing identifiers can be enough when readers couldn't work out who it was and the client is content with it. Abebe isn't, and these readers would know.
takeaway: If a client declines or would be recognizable, teach with fiction and label it.

topic: HIPAA: when it reaches a consultant
stem: For years a consultant has had a self-pay practice and, after checking with an attorney, treated it as outside HIPAA. A hospital's sports medicine clinic, which bills insurers, now hires her as an outside contractor. The clinic will send her its patients' confidence questionnaires and rehab charts, and she'll analyze them and report which rehab groups improve most. She won't meet the patients. Which rules should she expect to govern this information, in addition to the Ethics Code?
options: The same rules as her own practice, since HIPAA doesn't reach this work
HIPAA, through a business associate agreement with the clinic
HIPAA, as a covered provider that bills insurers electronically
A school's student-records rules, through a written agreement
rationales: This describes her self-pay practice. The clinic's charts are protected health information held by a covered entity, and they don't lose that status when sent to a contractor.
A contractor who analyzes identifiable patient information on behalf of a covered entity is acting as a business associate. HIPAA's safeguards follow the data to her through a written agreement.
Electronic billing of insurers is one way that a provider becomes covered. The clinic bills; she sends no claims.
School rules would be relevant if she handled records for a school. These are a hospital clinic's patients.
takeaway: HIPAA can reach a consultant through the data she handles for a covered entity, even if she never bills.
